newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - Croatian election won't hurt economic outlook - analysts.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Croatian election won't hurt economic outlook - analysts.

text.p: Croatia elects a new president on Sunday who will have the task of furthering economic reforms launched nearly four years ago, but analysts say the path to a market economy may be rocky as initial successes wear off.
The country has pulled away fast from its former Yugoslav neighbours and now boasts a strong currency, a low budget deficit and stable inflation rate of around 3.6 percent.

President Franjo Tudjman, widely expected to win Sunday's election, is credited for leaving economic management to technocrats and supporting their reforms. However analysts say problems remain and new challenges could rock the boat.
"On the macroeconomic level things are in a pretty good shape," Evan Kraft, American visiting scholar at Croatia's central bank told Reuters.
The key to continued progress now, he added, would be the freeing of domestic funds to spur development.

Kraft's view is similar to that of the World Bank which said recently that in order to secure healthy growth, Croatia has to encourage savings and investments on all levels. Real growth was estimated at a minimum five percent in 1996.
The bank suggested a target for investment by 2000 of 25 percent of the country's gross domestic product (GDP), currently estimated at some $18.5 billion.
However, savings are difficult to mobilise and intercompany debts continue to rise while a large portion of Croatian banks have limited resources, making capital expensive and hard to get.
In a bid to spur the economy, the central bank made a smaller cut in reserve requirements for banks this month.
But as it tries to stabilise increased inflows of hard currency which may spur inflation, it still has to keep a tight rein on money supply.

"The tourists are coming back in droves, which is always good news for the economy, but it's a headache for the National Bank because of the big inflow of foreign currency reserves," said James Oates at UBS in London.

"Inflation is going to be a problem because the bank has kept monetary policy very tight -- the inflow of funds has to be sterilised to prevent inflation," he added. "There is modest inflationary pressure but it isn't likely to be a big problem."
SLOW ECONOMIC REVIVAL MADE WORSE BY WAR

In such an environment long-term economic revival is extremely slow. But it was made worse in Croatia by the 1991-95 war that followed the break-up of Yugoslavia, which flattened infrastructure and scared away foreign investment and trade.

Industrial output is recovering at modest rates, rising 0.2 percent in April from March and 6.5 percent year-on-year. But all businesses, particularly export-oriented industries, are languishing under the weight of old debts and a stifling tax burden equivalent to more than 50 percent of GDP.
The average person earns a monthly net salary of 2,200 kuna ($360) and pensioners are even worse off.

"The medium-term agenda most people agree on is to decrease the level of government taxes and change the composition of expenditure over from the military towards the social and development-oriented expenditures," Kraft said.
Despite token cuts in defence spending following the end of the war, the military budget still consumes 6-7 percent of GDP.
Although the government plans to gradually ease the tax burden, other problems are expected to worsen.
Unemployment, though slightly lower at 16.6 percent in April than March, will rise if plans to restructure or even close some loss-making state firms are carried out.

Fewer than one fourth of all Croats hold registered jobs with taxes contributing to state coffers. Job creation is seen as a priority. Others include pension reform and further privatisation, which was delayed by the war.

"Privatisation is only a first step towards proper corporate governance," said Zarko Miljenovic, chief economist at the leading Croatian bank Zagrebacka Banka. He said there was no time to lose in the sell-off of large enterprises, which were nationalised at the start of the process six years ago.
After completed buyouts in small and medium-sized firms, some 50 percent of the economy is still in state hands and a voucher scheme to compensate war victims is only just starting.

There are plans to offer shares in the utilities, shipbuilding and some banks. Foreigners will probably be invited to buy up to 30 percent of the equity, providing considerable funds to finance post-war reconstruction.
Tourism too, Croatia's main hard currency earner, expects a brighter future with a return of foreign holiday-makers and its revenues will also come in handy.
But economists warn against what they describe as a "mixed blessing" of foreign capital inflows and new privatisation and debt issues.
Croatia has already won around $2 billion from official lenders and commercial sources since independence in 1991, raising fears about a crisis when debts come due for repayment.

Susanne Hallergard of ING Barings in London stressed the need to balance larger capital inflows against monetary and fiscal goals to prevent the economy from overheating. She said the kuna was already widely perceived to be overvalued.

"The government will have to be careful about how much the exchange rate appreciates and how (companies) maintain their competitiveness. If it appreciates too far, then you lose and have trouble exporting," Hallergard added.
The strong kuna has also hit the trade gap by spurring imports of capital goods and equipment, pushing it to $2.6 billion between January and April from $2.3 billion last year.
Croatia is likely to run another current account deficit this year as its services, income and current transfers together may not produce a large enough surplus to balance it.
But whatever the outlook, Sunday's election is not expected to change much on the financial scene even if politically there is a big upset and Tudjman loses to one of his two opponents.

"Nobody is going to change what has been economically a winning formula," said Oates. "Some positive things are definitely understated. The domestic economy is growing and inward investment is beginning to accelerate...You can be quite cautious about the future and still come up with impressive figures."
